instructions:
A PDF was filed by hand. Open the file at `attachments.pdf_path` and read it, then produce a structured summary.

Read it as a document, not as text: look at the figures, tables and plots. A result table usually settles what the paper actually achieved faster than the prose does, and a figure often carries the method. If the document is long, read the abstract, introduction, method and results sections in full and skim the rest.

`bibliography` must come from the document itself — its title page, header or footer. The filename is not evidence; it is whatever the person who saved the file happened to type.

`topics` is your judgement. These are the topics this archive tracks; list the slugs this paper genuinely belongs to, and leave the list empty rather than forcing a fit:
- reasoning-evaluation: Reasoning Evaluation — Benchmarks for reasoning and the methodology behind them: what each one actually tests, how contamination and memorization inflate a score, and where a reported gain fails to reproduce. The question the archive answers is which numbers a claim about reasoning can be built on.
- reasoning-faithfulness: Reasoning Faithfulness — The gap between a model's stated chain of thought and the computation that produced its answer: unfaithful or post-hoc rationalization, reasoning that is latent rather than written, encoded or steganographic traces, and what a monitor reading the trace can and cannot catch. The question the archive answers is when a visible reasoning trace is evidence about the model, and when it is only text.
- reasoning-interpretability: Reasoning Interpretability — What the computation behind reasoning looks like from the inside: circuits and the attention heads that carry them, features recovered by sparse dictionary learning, and the causal interventions used to establish that a component or a written state matters. The question the archive answers is which claims about a model's internal reasoning the available intervention methods can actually support, and at what granularity.
- reasoning-training: Reasoning Training — How a language model acquires long-form reasoning: reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, process versus outcome supervision, distillation of reasoning traces, and self-training. The question the archive answers is which training signal produces reasoning that generalizes, and what each one costs.
- test-time-scaling: Test-Time Scaling — What a model gains by thinking longer at inference: sampling and verification, search over reasoning steps, self-correction, and the length of the chain itself as a compute knob. The question the archive answers is how accuracy trades against tokens spent, and where that curve flattens.

`relevance` must have one entry per slug you listed in `topics`.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

bibliography.abstract: string - the paper's own abstract, verbatim
bibliography.arxiv_id: string - arXiv id if printed on the document, else empty
authors: string - author name, in the order printed
bibliography.doi: string - DOI if printed on the document, else empty
bibliography.title: string - the paper's own title, exactly as printed
bibliography.venue: string - journal, conference or 'preprint'; empty if unclear
bibliography.year: integer - publication year, 0 if the document does not say

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used. Not models: a checkpoint that was evaluated or fine-tuned belongs in `models`.
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
models: string - models the work trains, evaluates or analyses, as named in the paper (e.g. a base checkpoint, a released reasoning model, a judge)
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what
topics: string - slug of a tracked topic this paper belongs to; omit any that do not genuinely apply

payload.title: rethinking global convergence softmax pg linear function approximation

bibliography.abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods have played an essential role in the empirical successes of reinforcement learning. In order to handle large state-action spaces, PG methods are typically used with function approximation. In this setting, the approximation error in modeling problem-dependent quantities is a key notion for characterizing the global convergence of PG methods. We focus on Softmax PG with linear function approximation (referred to as Lin-SPG) and demonstrate that the approximation error is irrelevant to the algorithm's global convergence even for the stochastic bandit setting. Consequently, we first identify the necessary and sufficient conditions on the feature representation that can guarantee the asymptotic global convergence of Lin-SPG. Under these feature conditions, we prove that T iterations of Lin-SPG with a problem-specific learning rate result in an O(1/T) convergence to the optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove that Lin-SPG with any arbitrary constant learning rate can ensure asymptotic global convergence to the optimal policy.
bibliography.title: Rethinking the Global Convergence of Softmax Policy Gradient with Linear Function Approximation

contributions: A pair of four-armed bandit instances with nearly identical, and on rescaling exactly identical, approximation error on which softmax policy gradient converges to the optimum in one case and to a suboptimal arm in the other, both in the exact setting with no stochasticity -- establishing that approximation error cannot characterize global convergence and that the deciding factor is the feature representation.

Necessary and sufficient feature conditions for asymptotic global convergence in the exact setting: reward-ordering preservation under some linear transformation of the features, which alone is shown insufficient, strengthened to an inner-product condition on feature differences that must hold for every ordered triple of arms.

Convergence in the stochastic bandit setting under the same feature conditions, with a problem-specific constant learning rate giving monotonic improvement in expectation, almost-sure asymptotic convergence to the optimal policy, and an O(1/T) rate matching the known tabular result.

A proof technique that tracks differences between the logits of pairs of arms rather than each arm's dynamics separately, which recovers the tabular guarantee as a special case with a shorter argument.

Removal of the dependence on unknown problem constants: with any arbitrary constant learning rate the algorithm still converges asymptotically to the optimal policy, with average suboptimality decaying at O(ln(T)/T).
A counterexample to the non-domination condition of an existing published convergence theorem, together with a repaired condition for the three-arm case and its generalization.
result.limitations: The paper states no limitations section. The dominant scope fact is that everything is bandits: the state space is empty, so there is no sequential decision making, no credit assignment across a trajectory, and no discounting -- the paper is explicit that this is the simplest setting in which the question is already interesting, not a claim about MDPs. The policy is log-linear in a fixed feature matrix, which is one step past tabular and far from a neural network, and the feature dimension is required to be smaller than the number of arms. The feature conditions are conditions on the features and the reward ordering jointly, so they cannot be checked from a representation alone without already knowing which arm is best, which limits their use as a design criterion. Distinct mean rewards are assumed; the authors say they believe the results survive without it but do not prove it. The learning rate in the main stochastic theorems depends on the reward gap and on eigenvalues of the feature Gram matrix, none of which is available in practice, and the section that removes this dependence buys asymptotic convergence at a slower O(ln(T)/T) average rate rather than the O(1/T) of the tuned version. The empirical content is confined to the constructed examples and appendix figures; there is no experiment on a real task. Finally, the headline that approximation error is irrelevant is a statement about it failing to characterize convergence, not that a poor representation is harmless -- the second constructed instance fails precisely because of its features.
result.method: The setting is deliberately the simplest one in which the question is non-trivial: a K-armed stochastic bandit with an empty state space, distinct mean rewards, and a log-linear policy softmax(X*theta) built from a fixed feature matrix with fewer columns than arms, so the parameterization provably cannot represent every policy. The argument proceeds in three stages of increasing realism. First the exact setting, where the true mean rewards are known and the update is deterministic, is used to isolate the question from noise entirely: if the algorithm can fail here, the failure is a property of the features. Two four-armed, two-dimensional instances are constructed that differ only by swapping two columns of the feature matrix and are then compared, with the optimization landscape and the gradient trajectory plotted for each. Second, the feature condition is built up from the geometry those pictures suggest. The starting point is an existing condition, that some linear transformation of the features preserves the ordering of the rewards, which turns out to be necessary but not sufficient. It is strengthened by requiring the ordering to survive projection onto several orthogonal directions, which yields an inner-product condition on differences of feature vectors, first for three arms and then in general form for any three arms whose rewards are ordered. Under these conditions plus a learning rate bounded by the smoothness constant, the expected reward improves monotonically and the policy approaches a one-hot vector; convergence to the correct one-hot vector is then established by contradiction. Third, the stochastic setting replaces the known rewards with an on-policy importance-sampling estimator. Monotonic improvement in conditional expectation is recovered using unbiasedness, a strong growth condition bounding the gradient variance near stationary points, and a non-uniform smoothness property; almost-sure convergence follows by decomposing the logit process into a progress term and a noise term and showing the cumulative progress dominates. The proof works with differences of logits between pairs of arms rather than each arm separately, which the authors note shortens the tabular argument it generalizes. A final section removes the dependence on unknown problem constants in the learning rate.
result.one_liner: Shows by two four-armed bandits with nearly identical approximation error, one of which converges and one of which does not, that approximation error cannot characterize whether softmax policy gradient reaches the optimum, and replaces it with a condition on whether the features preserve the ordering of the rewards.
result.problem: Convergence guarantees for policy gradient under function approximation are almost always stated in the additive form suboptimality is at most optimization error plus approximation error, where the approximation error measures how well the feature span can represent the problem's quantities. That shape has a built-in weakness: if the features cannot represent the target exactly the bound never goes to zero, so it can never certify convergence to the optimum. The paper asks whether this is a real obstacle or an artefact of the analysis, and if the latter, what the right structural condition on the features is.

relevance.reasoning-training: Filed here for the same reason as the other convergence entries and with the same caveat: the paper is about bandits and never analyses a language model, so the transfer is the reader's to make. What makes it worth the shelf space is that it dismantles the metric the field reaches for by default. The intuition that a representation is good enough if it can approximate the target closely is exactly what the two constructed instances refute -- same approximation error, opposite outcomes, no noise involved -- and the replacement is a condition about whether the feature geometry preserves the ordering of rewards. Read against this archive's RLVR boundary dispute that is a suggestive formal analogue: whether policy gradient reaches the best action turns out to be a property of the representation rather than of the training signal or the amount of optimization, which is the same shape as the claim that RLVR is bounded by what the base model already encodes, stated somewhere it can be proved. The bandit restriction is less severe here than it first looks, because a single-prompt group-relative update with a terminal verifiable reward is structurally a bandit problem, though the paper does not make that connection itself. Two cautions travel with it. The feature conditions depend jointly on the features and on the reward ordering, so they diagnose rather than design -- one cannot check them without already knowing the answer. And the setting is unregularized, which puts it beside rather than inside the archive's entropy cluster: it says nothing about what an entropy term does to any of this.

result.results: The two constructed instances share a reward vector of (9,8,7,6) and differ only by a column swap. Their approximation errors are 14.2338 and 14.3178, and the paper notes they can be rescaled to be exactly equal without changing the behaviour, yet the algorithm converges to the optimal arm on the first and stalls at the arm with reward 8 on the second. Both are in the exact setting with no randomness at all. The approximation error in each case is far larger than any suboptimality gap in the problem, which is at most 3, so a bound of the additive form would be vacuous on the instance that does converge. The landscape plots show why: in the converging instance the plateaus are arranged so that gradient ascent can climb from reward 6 through 7 and 8 to 9, while in the other the plateau at reward 8 is surrounded by lower plateaus at 6 and 7, trapping the trajectory. The replacement condition is that some linear transformation of the features preserves the reward ordering, strengthened to an inner-product condition on feature differences; under it, convergence to the optimal policy is proved for three arms and then for any number. In the stochastic setting the same feature conditions give almost-sure asymptotic global convergence, and a rate of O(1/T) that matches the known tabular rate. Because those learning rates depend on unknown quantities including the reward gap, a final result removes the dependence: with any arbitrary constant learning rate the algorithm still converges asymptotically, with average suboptimality decaying at O(ln(T)/T). The tabular case is recovered as the special instance where the feature matrix is the identity, which the paper checks satisfies its feature condition. One further result is worth recording on its own: the paper reports that the non-domination condition of an existing published theorem is not sufficient for global convergence from any initialization, constructs a counterexample to it, and shows its own feature condition repairs the proof for three arms before generalizing.
